title.title: Zero-Knowledge & Privacy
title.subtitle: Prove what matters, reveal nothing else — what ZK and privacy unlock for business

privacy.heading: A public chain is not private
privacy.subtitle: Every address, balance and transfer is visible to anyone, forever. Pseudonymous is not anonymous: one link to your name unlocks your whole history. Off-chain, a salary or a bank statement is private by default; wanting the same on-chain is normal, not suspicious.

zkp.heading: Zero-Knowledge Proofs — the one idea
zkp.subtitle: One sentence and one everyday example.
zkp.oneLinerB: without revealing anything that makes it true.
zkp.exampleSubtitle: Same goal, two ways. Watch what the bouncer learns.
zkp.withoutBodyStrong: name, address, nationality and exact birth date
zkp.withoutCaption: You proved one fact and leaked five.

demo.idle: Choose an option on the left…

zkpCave.heading: Where's Waldo? — the same idea, visually
zkpCave.subtitle: I prove I found Waldo on a crowded page without telling you where he is.

steps.title: The claim
steps.text: I say I found Waldo on this crowded page. You don't believe me, and I refuse to point, because that gives my answer away.

steps.title: The proof
steps.text: I cover the whole page with a large opaque sheet that has one tiny Waldo-sized hole, lined up exactly over him. You see Waldo through the hole.

steps.title: You're convinced
steps.text: Waldo is clearly on the page. But the sheet hid the rest, so you still have no idea where on the page he is.

zkpCave.punchlineA: you end fully convinced Waldo is there, yet learn
zkpCave.punchlineB: about his location. That gap is "zero-knowledge".
zkpCave.classicBody: "the magic cave": Alice repeatedly exits the side a verifier shouts, proving she knows the password without ever saying it. Repeat enough and luck is ruled out.

zkIdentity.heading: KYC without handing over your identity
zkIdentity.subtitle: Step by step. Any ZK-capable platform can run this pattern.

steps.label: Bank issues a credential
steps.desc: Your bank verifies you once and signs a digital credential: name, date of birth, residency, sanctions check. It lives in your wallet — only you hold it.

steps.label: You generate a proof
steps.desc: Your wallet builds a proof: "signed by the bank · age ≥ 18 · EU resident · not sanctioned." The proof contains none of the raw data.

steps.label: The app verifies
steps.desc: The app's smart contract checks the proof and lets you in. Your name and birth date never leave your wallet — not even the app operator can read them.

business: No database of passports to leak — far less GDPR exposure
Onboarding in seconds, reusable across every service that trusts the issuer
Regulators still get what they need: proof the check was done, on demand
zkIdentity.footStrong: private voting · proof of solvency · medical records · sanctions screening
zkIdentity.footB: — anywhere the question is "is this true?" without "who are you?".

zkJobs.heading: One proof, two jobs — privacy and scale
zkJobs.subtitle: The same kind of proof answers two different questions. Mixing them up is the most common misunderstanding about ZK.

rows.v: Yes. That is the whole point.
Private payments, age and eligibility checks, compliance proofs.
Redoing thousands of transactions one by one.
No. Every transaction is still public.
ZK rollups (zkSync, Starknet, Linea, Scroll): fees of a few cents. Also called a validity proof.

sort.label: Which job is ZK doing here?

items.text: A bar's door app confirms you are over 18 and never sees your ID.
items.why: The data stays hidden; only the yes or no gets out.

items.text: A network bundles 5,000 payments and gives Ethereum one small proof that all of them were valid.
items.why: Nothing is hidden. Ethereum just skips re-running 5,000 payments.

items.text: An exchange shows it holds every customer's deposit without publishing a single balance.
items.why: Balances stay confidential; the total is proven.

items.text: You pay a few cents on a "ZK rollup", and your transfer still shows up on a public block explorer.
items.why: A ZK rollup is cheap, not private. The name describes the proof, not secrecy.

zkLimits.heading: Reality check — what a ZK proof does not do
zkLimits.subtitle: A proof answers one question and stops there. Four claims you will hear, and where each one goes too far.
zkLimits.hint: Tap a claim to check it.

items.claim: It uses ZK, so it is private.
items.reality: Only what the designers chose to hide is hidden. Everything else on a public chain stays public, and a ZK rollup hides nothing at all.
items.tag: Private on purpose, never by default

items.claim: The proof checks out, so the fact is true.
items.reality: A proof shows the claim follows from its inputs. If the bank signed a wrong birth date, the proof still passes. You are still trusting the issuer: the oracle problem again (Section 05).
items.tag: Trust moves to the issuer; it does not vanish

items.claim: A shielded payment cannot be traced.
items.reality: The proof hides what is inside it, not the clues around it: when the money went in, how much, when it came out. With only a few users, those clues are enough.
items.tag: Hiding in a crowd needs a crowd

items.claim: With ZK, the product is compliant.
items.reality: ZK is a tool, not a licence. The same maths runs a compliance proof and a mixer; what the law makes of a product depends on how it is designed and used.
items.tag: Lawful by design, not by maths

zkLimits.givesLabel: What a proof does give you
zkLimits.givesStrong: One statement, checked, with nothing extra revealed.
zkLimits.givesBody: What gets hidden, whether the inputs are honest and whether the use is lawful are still decisions people make.

privacyApproaches.heading: Four ways to get privacy on-chain
privacyApproaches.subtitle: Each makes a different trade-off between strength, flexibility, and how regulators treat it.

items.name: Zcash
items.mech: Optional shielded transactions use zk-SNARKs to prove ownership and value conservation without revealing sender, recipient or amount.
items.trade: Privacy is opt-in, so most volume stays transparent — weakening the anonymity set.

items.name: Monero
items.mech: Mandatory privacy: ring signatures hide the sender, stealth addresses hide the recipient, RingCT hides the amount.
items.trade: No transparency option — auditing is hard, so many exchanges have delisted it.

items.name: Aztec · Aleo
items.mech: Smart contracts with private state and inputs — build any confidential dApp, not just private payments.
items.trade: Far more flexible, but newer tooling (Noir, Leo) and privacy lives at the contract level.

items.name: Mixers
items.mech: Pool many deposits, withdraw to fresh addresses — breaking the on-chain link between sender and receiver.
items.trade: Credibly neutral and immutable — which is exactly why they became a sanctions target.

privacyRegulation.heading: Tornado Cash — when privacy code met the law
privacyRegulation.subtitle: One mixer, one sanction, and years of courts deciding where a privacy tool ends and laundering infrastructure begins.

story.d: A non-custodial mixer on Ethereum: deposit, wait, withdraw to a fresh address. Nobody operates it — the code simply runs.
The US Treasury sanctioned the smart-contract addresses themselves — a first. Its reason: ~$7B laundered, including $455M by North Korea's Lazarus Group. Ordinary users were swept in too.
Alexey Pertsev convicted in the Netherlands (64 months, under appeal); Roman Storm awaiting trial in the US. Writing privacy software itself became the legal question.
A US appeals court ruled immutable smart contracts are not "property" that can be sanctioned. OFAC delisted Tornado Cash on 21 March 2025.
Storm convicted on one count (unlicensed money transmission); the jury hung on laundering and sanctions charges. Samourai Wallet's founders received 4–5 years (Nov 2025).

privacyRegulation.truthsLabel: Two things are true at once
privacyRegulation.truthA: Privacy tools really did shield a state-sponsored hacking group's loot. Regulators had a genuine problem.
privacyRegulation.truthB: The same tools protected ordinary people from surveillance — and sanctioning code punished users who had done nothing wrong.
privacyRegulation.cypherpunk: The Cypherpunks (Course 01) said privacy is a precondition for freedom; regulators say untraceable money is a precondition for crime. Both are partly right, which is why selective disclosure (next slide) matters.
privacyRegulation.recapFreedom: Course 01 · Prologue — the Cypherpunks: privacy as a precondition for freedom
privacyRegulation.guidanceC: (e.g. prove "not on a sanctions list" without revealing identity) over all-or-nothing anonymity.

quiz.question: A lender must confirm that an applicant earns at least €40,000 a year before approving a loan. What does a zero-knowledge approach change?
options: The payslip is encrypted and stored on-chain, so only the lender can open it.
The applicant sends a proof that "income ≥ €40,000, attested by a trusted issuer" is true. The lender verifies the proof and never sees the payslip or the exact figure.
The lender no longer needs to check anything: the blockchain guarantees the applicant is honest.
The salary is hidden from everyone, regulators included, forever.
quiz.explanation: Zero-knowledge separates the claim from the data behind it. A trusted issuer (an employer or a bank) signs the facts once; the applicant's wallet turns them into a proof of one statement; the lender checks the proof. Nothing is stored on-chain in readable or encrypted form, a check still happens, and the applicant can produce further proofs for a regulator on demand. That is selective disclosure, not blanket secrecy.

public.question: A company pays salaries in stablecoins from a single wallet on a public chain. One employee mentions their wallet address to a friend. What can the friend now see?
options: Nothing: addresses are anonymous, so payments cannot be tied to a person.
Only the most recent payment to that employee; older ones are archived.
The employee's whole payment history and, by following the paying wallet, what every other address on the payroll receives.
Nothing, unless the friend runs a validator node.
public.explanation: A public chain is pseudonymous, not anonymous: one link between an address and a name opens the whole trail, in both directions, for good. Privacy has to be added on purpose.

jobs.question: A payments start-up moves to a "ZK rollup" and tells customers their transactions are now private. Is that claim right?
options: No. Here the proof shows Ethereum that a batch of transactions was processed correctly, so it need not redo them; the transactions themselves stay public.
Yes. Any system that uses zero-knowledge proofs hides sender, receiver and amount.
Yes. The transactions run off Ethereum, so nobody can see them any more.
Only partly: amounts are hidden, but senders and receivers are public.
jobs.explanation: ZK has two jobs. In a rollup it is a validity proof, which buys cheap checking, not secrecy. Privacy has to be designed in separately.

issuer.question: An app receives a valid zero-knowledge proof of "over 18, credential signed by Bank X". What has the app actually established?
options: The user's exact date of birth, in a form only the app can read.
That the user is over 18 with mathematical certainty, whoever issued the credential.
Nothing: a zero-knowledge proof reveals no information at all, not even whether the claim holds.
That Bank X vouched for it and the proof matches that credential. If Bank X got it wrong, the proof still passes.
issuer.explanation: A proof guarantees the claim follows from its inputs, not that the inputs are true. Trust moves to the issuer; it does not disappear.

crowd.question: A privacy pool has had three users this month. On Monday one of them deposits 100 ETH; on Tuesday 100 ETH is withdrawn to a new address. No cryptography is broken. What is the lesson?
options: The proof must be faulty: a valid zero-knowledge proof makes this kind of guess impossible.
The proof hid the link, but timing, amount and a tiny crowd give it away. Privacy depends on how many others you hide among.
Nothing leaks: deposits into and withdrawals from the pool are invisible to observers.
The pool's operator must have disclosed who the users are.
crowd.explanation: ZK hides what is inside the proof, not the clues around it. With few users and matching amounts, an observer can make a confident guess without breaking any maths.

tornado.question: The US Treasury sanctioned Tornado Cash in 2022 and lifted the sanction in 2025 after a court ruling. What does the episode best illustrate?
options: Privacy tools are used only by criminals, which is why the sanction was imposed.
Regulators had no real problem to solve: nothing illicit ever passed through the mixer.
The same tool hid stolen funds and protected lawful users, and with all-or-nothing anonymity nobody could stop one without hitting the other.
Once code is sanctioned a government can switch it off, so the contracts stopped running.
tornado.explanation: Both were true at once: stolen funds were laundered through it, including hundreds of millions of dollars by North Korea's Lazarus Group, and lawful users were swept in, while the contracts kept running. That is the case for selective disclosure.

takeaways.title: Section 07 — Key Takeaways
items: A public chain is transparent by default: one link between a wallet and a name exposes its whole history — a real obstacle for payroll, suppliers and treasury
Zero-knowledge in one line: prove a statement is true without revealing what makes it true
ZK has two jobs: keep data private, or prove that heavy work was done correctly (ZK rollups). The second makes a chain cheaper, not private
It is already in production: private payments, proof of reserves, private voting, and KYC where the customer proves only what each service needs, with no passport database to leak
A proof settles one statement: nothing is private unless it was designed to be, a proof is only as honest as its inputs, and a small crowd hides no one

Privacy is a legitimate need and a laundering risk at once: Tornado Cash showed that all-or-nothing anonymity collides with the law, and selective, provable disclosure is what lets regulated business use public chains

keyPoints.s7-public: A public ledger is a permanent record; privacy has to be added on purpose.
keyPoints.s7-zk: Prove it is true without showing why.
keyPoints.s7-waldo: A proof convinces by making cheating impossible, not by showing the secret.
keyPoints.s7-kyc: Verify the claim, not the person: the issuer vouches once and the customer reveals only what each service needs.
keyPoints.s7-live: ZK is a product, not a paper: payments, solvency, identity and compliance proofs are live today.
keyPoints.s7-jobs: ZK can hide the data or skip the re-checking. A ZK rollup does the second: it is cheap, not private.
keyPoints.s7-limits: A proof settles one statement. What stays hidden, and whether the inputs are honest, is still a design choice.
keyPoints.s7-approaches: Mixers hide everything or nothing; ZK reveals exactly what a counterparty needs.
keyPoints.s7-tornado: Untraceable money shields dissidents and launderers alike; selective disclosure is the way out.
keyPoints.s7-disclosure: Keep the data confidential and still prove you follow the rules.
